title: Statistical estimation of probable maximum precipitation
authors: Martin, A., Fournier, É., Jalbert, J.

figure.caption: Simulation test with a rainfall-like (convex) distribution whose true upper bound is 50 (dashed line). Dots show the average estimate of the upper bound ψ — the PMP — over 100 synthetic samples and thin lines the 95% range, for (a) the method of moments, (b) maximum likelihood and (c) Bayesian estimation, as sample size grows. Only the method of moments stays near the truth, and even it scatters widely.
figure.credit: Figure 2 from Martin et al. (2025), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Turning the official definition of probable maximum precipitation (PMP) into a proper statistical model shows that the 'upper limit' of rainfall can barely be pinned down from data — so the authors advise against their own model and recommend extreme-value analysis with stated uncertainty instead.
background: PMP is the theoretical largest rainfall that could fall over an area, and it is used to design structures whose failure would be catastrophic, such as large dams and nuclear facilities. The usual ways of estimating it — moisture maximization of past storms and Hershfield's empirical formula — involve subjective choices (which storms to pick, how to estimate precipitable water, whether to cap the maximization ratio), rarely come with an uncertainty range, and cannot easily include climate change. There is also a basic tension: PMP assumes rainfall has an upper bound, while rainfall records usually behave as if they are heavy-tailed and unbounded.
approach: Starting from the WMO moisture-maximization formula, the authors show that daily rainfall can be written as a fraction between 0 and 1 multiplied by the PMP. That leads naturally to the Pearson Type-I distribution (a Beta distribution stretched to the interval from 0 to the PMP), in which the PMP is simply a parameter to be estimated. They tested three estimators — method of moments, maximum likelihood and Bayesian — on synthetic samples with a known upper bound, then applied the model to May–October daily rainfall at two stations 26 km apart in Quebec, Canada: Montréal airport (1953–2024) and St. Hubert airport (1949–2024). The results were compared with moisture maximization, Hershfield's method (K = 15) and a 60 000-year return level from a peaks-over-threshold extreme-value model.
findings: For rainfall-shaped (convex) distributions the upper bound and one shape parameter can compensate for each other, so very different PMP values fit the data almost equally well. Maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimates became unusable; they only stabilised at sample sizes around 40 000 wet days, roughly 400 years of record.
The method of moments gave realistic values on average, but for individual samples the estimate ranged from less than half to more than twice the true bound.

For real data the model gave a PMP of 270 mm at Montréal and 417 mm at St. Hubert, close to the moisture-maximization values (about 280 mm and 436 mm) but with very wide bootstrap uncertainty — and a large gap between two stations that share essentially the same climate.

The extreme-value model fitted both stations well and gave consistent 60 000-year rainfall: 185 mm (95% interval 114–363) at Montréal and 200 mm (120–385) at St. Hubert. Its shape parameter was positive at both sites, pointing to an unbounded heavy tail.

The authors therefore do not recommend the Pearson Type-I model for practice. In line with the 2024 U.S. National Academies report, they favour choosing an explicit, very low exceedance probability from extreme-value analysis and always reporting its confidence interval.
relevance: PMP and the probable maximum flood derived from it decide how large the spillways of major dams must be, so they sit behind the safety of everyone living downstream. This paper is an honest 'negative result': it shows that a single hard number for the 'largest possible rainfall' is far more fragile than it looks, and that two nearby gauges can give very different answers for numerical rather than physical reasons. Korea also relies on PMP for dam design and for re-evaluating older dams as monsoon and typhoon rainfall intensifies, so the message applies directly: treat PMP as an estimate with a wide range, not a guaranteed ceiling. For students, it is a clear lesson in why a design value should always come with its uncertainty.

title: Diurnal variability of global precipitation: insights from hourly satellite and reanalysis datasets
authors: Pradhan, R. K., Markonis, Y., Marra, F., Nikolopoulos, E. I., Papalexiou, S. M., Levizzani, V.

figure.caption: Average daily cycle (local solar time, 2001–2020) of precipitation (a) amount, (b) frequency and (c) intensity for the globe, land and ocean, as seen by four satellite products and the ERA5 reanalysis. The curves share a similar shape for amount but sit far apart for frequency and intensity.
figure.credit: Figure 5 from Pradhan et al. (2025), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Five widely used hourly precipitation datasets agree fairly well on when and how much it rains over a day, but disagree strongly on how often and how hard it rains — ERA5 in particular rains too often and too gently.
background: Many flood and water-resources studies now rely on gridded precipitation from satellites or reanalysis, especially where gauges are sparse. These products are known to be less reliable at sub-daily scales than at daily or monthly scales, and climate models also struggle to reproduce the daily rhythm of rainfall. Yet few studies had compared several products worldwide at the hourly scale, so users had little guidance on which features of the diurnal cycle they can trust.
approach: The authors compared four satellite products (IMERG, GSMaP, CMORPH and PERSIANN) with the ERA5 reanalysis over 60° S–60° N for the common period 2001–2020. All data were brought to the same 0.25° hourly grid and converted from UTC to local solar time. For each grid cell they computed three quantities for every hour of the day: mean amount, frequency of wet hours (at least 0.1 mm per hour) and intensity during wet hours. They then mapped the hour of the daily peak and used k-means clustering with four clusters to group regions with similar diurnal shapes.
findings: All five datasets show the classic pattern: rainfall over land peaks in the afternoon (mostly 15:00–18:00 local time), while rainfall over the ocean peaks in the early morning (about 02:00–06:00).
ERA5 peaks earlier than the satellite products over land — around 15:00 local time, compared with 16:00–18:00 for most of the others.

ERA5 rains far too often: its wet-hour frequency in the tropical rain belt is about 40%, roughly double that of the satellite products (below 20%), and its intensity is correspondingly the lowest over the ocean.

The size of the afternoon land peak differs widely between products, from about 0.18 mm/h in ERA5 down to less than 0.1 mm/h in GSMaP; CMORPH gives the highest intensities and GSMaP the lowest over land.
Differences between datasets are largest in the Southern Hemisphere mid-to-high latitudes, and IMERG and CMORPH agree most closely on peak timing.
relevance: Short, intense bursts of rain are what cause flash floods and urban flooding, so the timing, frequency and intensity of hourly rainfall matter as much as the daily total. This study shows that a product can give a reasonable daily amount while still spreading it over too many gentle hours, which would make a flood model underestimate peak flows. For Korea, where summer monsoon and typhoon rain often falls in a few violent hours and many small basins have no gauge, it is a reminder to check satellite or reanalysis rainfall against local observations before using it for design or warning. Students and engineers can take away a simple habit: look at amount, frequency and intensity separately, not just the total.

title: A 3D-Based Method for Flood Depth Estimation From Social Media Images
authors: Shen, M., Zhang, F., Shi, Y.

figure.caption: Workflow of the method. A flood photo from social media is matched to a 3D city model to recover where the camera was and how it was pointed, the water's edge is segmented in the photo, and the edge points are then placed in 3D space so that subtracting the ground elevation gives the flood depth.
figure.credit: Figure 2 from Shen et al. (2026), Water Resources Research, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: By lining up flood photos posted on social media with a 3D model of the city, water depth can be measured against the buildings themselves, to within about 0.16 m on average, even when no person, car or sign is in the picture to serve as a ruler.
background: In a dense city, the damage a flood causes depends more on how deep the water is than on how far it spreads, yet street-level depth sensors are sparse. Photos and videos posted during a flood come from many locations and arrive quickly, but most methods for reading depth from them need a reference object of known size, such as a person, a vehicle or a traffic sign. Those objects are often missing or only partly visible, and their real size is uncertain. City-wide 3D models, which more and more cities now publish, offer a stable metric reference instead, but social media photos come without the camera position needed to align them.
approach: The authors built a pipeline with three parts: a 2D–3D matching model called Obj-CoFi, a flood extraction step, and a depth calculation. Obj-CoFi first segments both the photo and the 3D point cloud into objects (using pre-trained models such as SAM and Mask3D), matches them coarsely object-to-object with a transformer, then refines the match to pixel level by rendering each 3D object from several viewpoints and matching those renderings to the photo; the camera pose follows from PnP-RANSAC. The water area is segmented with the pre-trained SEEM model, and the water-edge pixels are projected into 3D to read their elevation. The matching model was trained and tested on the Aachen Day-Night urban benchmark (6,381 samples), and the full method was applied to 62 geolocated images collected from X during the extreme rainstorm of 7–8 September 2023 in Hong Kong, using the city's 3D photo-realistic model. Depth estimates were compared with a reference-object geometric method (ROG) and a vision language model (GPT-5).
findings: On the urban benchmark, Obj-CoFi clearly outperformed the 2D3D-MATR baseline: the mean fine inlier ratio rose from 9.2% to 39.6% and the registration recall from 8.6% to 24.2%.

Both design choices were needed. Object-level partitioning raised coarse matching accuracy, but pixel-level matching only improved once the rendering-based (mesh-based) fine matching was added, and using six rendered views per object worked best.
Across the Hong Kong images the method reached a mean absolute error of 0.164 m and a root mean square error of 0.212 m.

Only about 30% of the images contained a usable reference object. On those, the reference-object method was slightly better (MAE 0.145 m versus 0.152 m); on the remaining 70% it could not be applied, while the 3D-based method still reached an MAE of 0.171 m compared with 0.261 m for the vision language model, whose answers also varied between repeated runs.

Depth maps for seven districts showed the deepest and most extensive flooding in Wong Tai Sin and Wan Chai. Rainfall was similar across the districts, so the differences were attributed mainly to flat terrain, impervious commercial land use and older drainage. The flooded areas were broadly consistent with a Sentinel-1 image, but the authors note that the depths themselves still need checking against in situ measurements.
relevance: When streets flood, the first evidence is usually a stream of phone photos, long before any survey team arrives. This study shows a way to turn those photos into actual depth numbers and maps, which can help emergency teams decide which roads and underpasses are dangerous and later give modellers the observations they need to calibrate urban flood models. The idea is relevant to Korean cities, where intense monsoon and typhoon downpours can quickly flood low-lying streets and basements and where city-scale 3D models are becoming more widely available. It is also worth keeping the limits in mind: the test used 62 images from a single event, the reference depths were annotated by hand, and the method only maps places that someone happened to photograph.

title: Testing discharge assimilation strategies to enhance short-range AI-based operational rainfall–runoff forecasts
authors: Saint-Fleur, B. E., Gaume, E., Surmont, F., Akil, N., Theriez, D.

figure.caption: The three ways of feeding recently observed river flow into a forecast. A small neural network (MLP) either forecasts flow on its own from weather data and past observed flow (DA1), also receives the flow simulated by an LSTM or by the SAC-SMA model (DA2), or forecasts the error of those models so that it can be corrected (DA3).
figure.credit: Figure 2 from Saint-Fleur et al. (2026), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Telling a streamflow forecast what the river did in the last few days clearly improves short-range predictions, and once realistic ensemble weather forecasts are used, a simple neural network fed with recent flow can beat a much more sophisticated LSTM.
background: Operational flood and water-supply forecasting has long relied on 'discharge assimilation': using the latest river-gauge readings to pull a running forecast back toward reality. Deep learning rainfall–runoff models, especially LSTMs, now often outperform traditional models, but most published studies run them without this step and test them with observed weather rather than real weather forecasts. That leaves an open question for forecasting centres: how much does recent observed flow add to an AI model, and do the results still hold when the weather input is uncertain?
approach: The authors used a multilayer perceptron (MLP) as a light 'orchestrator' and tested three assimilation strategies: the MLP alone with weather data and past observed flow (DA1), the MLP plus forecasts from a pre-trained rainfall–runoff model (DA2), and an MLP that predicts and corrects that model's errors (DA3). The two benchmark models were a regional LSTM and the conceptual SAC-SMA model, evaluated on the CAMELS-US catchments, with a further test on French catchments from CAMELS-FR. Separate models were built for lead times of 1 to 7 days. Forecasts were first run with 'perfect' weather (observed values used as the forecast) and then with ensemble weather inputs, including a no-skill climatology ensemble and hindcast or archived forecast ensembles. Skill was measured with NSE, KGE and a persistence score for single forecasts, and with CRPS, rank diagrams, spread–skill ratio, Brier score and AUC for ensembles.
findings: With perfect weather input, adding recent observed flow improved forecasts, with the size of the gain depending on how good the benchmark already was and on lead time; the benefit shrank as lead time grew.
The conceptual SAC-SMA model gained consistently, while the LSTM gained mainly at short lead times and in basins where it had performed poorly to begin with.

Combining the MLP with a rainfall–runoff model's forecast (DA2) was the most effective strategy overall, followed by error correction (DA3); both improved the benchmarks or at least did not significantly degrade them.

With ensemble weather forecasts the ranking changed: the simple MLP with observed flow (DA1) outperformed the LSTM across the tested lead times, particularly in detecting threshold exceedances (Brier score and AUC).

The LSTM's flow ensembles were too narrow (under-dispersed), even when driven by a wide climatology ensemble, and in the French catchments, which respond more slowly, assimilation stayed useful at longer lead times.
relevance: A model that wins a benchmark with observed rainfall is not automatically the best one to run in a real forecasting room, where tomorrow's rain is uncertain; this study shows that the ranking can flip once that uncertainty is included. For flood warning it is a reminder that the river gauge itself is one of the most valuable inputs, and that even a small, cheap neural network can go a long way when it sees the latest observations. This is encouraging for places like Korea, where many basins are small and react within hours to monsoon and typhoon rain, and where agencies need forecasts that are fast, affordable and honest about their uncertainty. For students, the take-away is to evaluate forecasts the way they will actually be used: with forecast weather, with ensembles, and with checks on whether the spread is trustworthy.

title: What is a drought-to-flood transition? Pitfalls and recommendations for defining consecutive hydrological extreme events
authors: Anderson, B. J., Muñoz-Castro, E., Tallaksen, L. M., Matano, A., Götte, J., Armitage, R., Magee, E., Brunner, M. I.

figure.caption: How the events are picked from a daily streamflow record. Left: the flow is smoothed before droughts are identified (a), and rivers that run dry get a special ranking so zero-flow days can be handled (b). Right: the same record analysed with a drought threshold that changes every day (c), by season (d) or stays fixed (e); brown bars are detected droughts, blue dots are floods, and each choice selects different droughts, so a 'rapid transition' appears only in some cases.
figure.credit: Figure 2 from Anderson et al. (2025), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Whether a river is counted as having swung from drought to flood depends heavily on how you define drought, flood and the time gap between them, and common definitions picked up only three of eight real, well-reported drought-to-flood events.
background: Floods that arrive right after a drought make headlines and can be especially damaging, so research on these 'whiplash' events is growing fast. But droughts and floods have traditionally been studied separately, each with its own definitions, and there is no agreed way to define the two happening back to back. If different studies use different rules, their counts and trends cannot really be compared, and events that hurt people may not even show up in the statistics.
approach: The authors chose eight catchments in seven countries (Australia, Chile, England, Italy, Norway, Switzerland, and California and Texas in the USA) where a drought-to-flood event with real impacts was reported by media, agencies or scientists. Using observed daily streamflow, they detected droughts with three threshold styles (changing daily through the year, changing by season, or fixed) and floods with a seasonal or fixed peaks-over-threshold. Thresholds were tuned so every method gave the same event frequency, about one drought every two years and two floods per year, which makes the methods comparable. A transition was counted when a flood began less than 90 days after a drought ended, with 14 days marking a 'rapid' transition, and the gaps were fitted with a GEV distribution to estimate how likely a transition is within those windows. They then checked whether each method found the reported events and looked at the time series to understand the failures.
findings: Only three of the eight reported drought-to-flood events were detected. In Switzerland, England, Italy and California no method combination found the transition, while in Texas and Australia every combination did.
The Norwegian event was caught only with the daily varying drought threshold and the Chilean one only with the fixed threshold, so the 'right' method differs from river to river.

Method choice mattered most in strongly seasonal rivers: in Norway the estimated chance of a flood within 14 days of a drought ending ranged from 4.1 % to 12.7 % depending on the thresholds. In weakly seasonal rivers such as the Swiss one it mattered little (14.7–19.8 %).

Daily averages can hide flash floods: in the Swiss Emme the daily flow on the flood day was not extreme, but the hourly peak reached 255 m³/s, and the river went from low flow to flood and back in under 12 hours.

The authors conclude that no single definition fits all rivers and recommend choosing methods to match the impact of interest, filtering events by season or driver, and defining transitions relative to what is normal for each catchment.
relevance: 'Drought-to-flood' or 'weather whiplash' is now a common phrase in news and research, but this paper shows that the numbers behind it depend strongly on definitions that are rarely questioned. That is a useful lesson for anyone reading or producing statistics on extremes: check how the event was defined and whether the data resolution can even see it. Korea is a natural place for these swings, with dry springs followed by the monsoon and typhoons, strongly seasonal flow, and many small, steep basins where floods rise and fall within hours, exactly the conditions where the study found thresholds and daily data most likely to mislead. For water managers who must switch reservoirs from saving water to making flood room, a clear, locally meaningful definition of such transitions is the first step toward planning for them.

title: Advancing Near-Real-Time Flood Inundation Mapping in Australia
authors: Hou, J., Sharples, W., Tarpanelli, A., Renzullo, L., Woldemeskel, F., Carrara, E.

figure.caption: One flooded river reach in the Hawkesbury-Nepean Valley seen by different sources: Sentinel-2 true colour and NDWI with cloud mask (a, b), Sentinel-1 VV and VH radar backscatter (c, d), the Copernicus GloFAS GFM flood map (e) and the Landsat-based DEA Water Observations (f), compared with the LiDAR elevation model (g) and the study's 5 m flood depth map (h). Clouds, riverbank trees and data gaps leave holes in (a–f) that the terrain-based approach fills in.
figure.credit: Figure 7 from Hou et al. (2026), Water Resources Research, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: By converting a water level, whether measured at a gauge, simulated by a model or inferred from a satellite image, into flood extent and depth on 1 m airborne LiDAR terrain, Australia can get detailed 5 m flood maps in near real time even when clouds or missing gauges leave gaps.
background: Flooding causes about a fifth of natural-hazard deaths in Australia, and the 2022 floods alone cost around 5 billion dollars. During an event, managers need to know quickly where the water is and how deep it is. Gauges only give point measurements and can fail or be missing, optical satellites are blinded by the clouds that come with heavy rain, radar has its own problems with trees and buildings, and large-scale models are uncalibrated in many places. No single source is enough on its own.
approach: The authors built a cloud-based workflow that pulls live gauge water levels through the Bureau of Meteorology's data API, daily runoff from the national AWRA-L water balance model routed with the CaMa-Flood river model, and Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery from Google Earth Engine and Digital Earth Australia. All three paths end in the same step: a Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) map built from 1 m airborne LiDAR and corrected with national river and historical water datasets, which turns a water level into a 5 m map of flood extent and depth. For satellite images, they search for the water level whose HAND footprint best matches the raw satellite flood map, which fills areas hidden by cloud, trees or missing data. Model uncertainty was handled with 100 ensemble runs varying channel width and Manning roughness, giving probabilistic maps. The system was tested on seven flood-prone catchments in Queensland and New South Wales, and checked against commercial ICEYE flood maps where they were available.
findings: For the December 2023 floods after Tropical Cyclone Jasper, gauge-based maps agreed best with the ICEYE benchmark (critical success index 0.81–0.85), and Sentinel-1 maps scored 0.80–0.81 in the two rivers where radar caught the flood.
Model-based maps worked well in some rivers (CSI 0.81–0.85 in the Daintree and Mulgrave) but failed in the Barron (0.14), where no satellite image was available to fill the gap either.
Optical satellites saw nothing useful in the four Queensland rivers because of heavy cloud, so cloud-penetrating radar and the model were the only alternatives to gauges.

In the March 2022 Hawkesbury-Nepean flood, combining several satellite passes tracked flooded area more closely than the model median (RMSE about 8.6 versus 18.2 km² against the gauge-based series), mainly because the satellites captured the recession, which the model simulated too slowly.

Of the uncertain model parameters, Manning roughness affected flood timing and size much more than bankfull width, and adding runoff ensembles helped the model reproduce flood peaks in hindcast tests.
relevance: When a flood hits, the most useful product is a map of where the water is right now and how deep, not just a river level at one bridge. This study shows that the key ingredient is a very detailed terrain model: once you have it, a single water level from any source can be turned into a street-scale flood map. Korea has the same pieces available, with dense gauge networks on major rivers, national LiDAR elevation data and free Sentinel-1 radar that sees through monsoon and typhoon clouds, while small and ungauged streams remain the hard case. The paper is also an honest reminder that models can miss badly in some rivers, so combining sources and showing uncertainty matters as much as the map itself.

title: Rainfall intensity estimations based on degradation characteristics of images taken with commercial cameras

figure.caption: Workflow of the method: image patches are processed with the dark channel prior to get transmission, scene depth comes from camera settings and topography, and the two together give an extinction coefficient that is converted into rainfall intensity.
figure.credit: Figure 4 from Kanazawa and Uchida (2025), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Rain makes distant scenery look hazier in a camera image, and by measuring how much the background fades with distance, ordinary outdoor cameras can give a physically based estimate of rainfall intensity without any training data.
background: Rain gauges are sparse, especially in mountains, and radar or satellite products struggle to resolve rainfall at the scale of a small watershed. Meanwhile, surveillance and monitoring cameras are everywhere. Most camera-based rainfall methods so far rely on spotting raindrop streaks or on machine-learning models that need large labelled datasets. This study asks whether the overall 'washing out' of a background scene during rain can be turned into a rainfall estimate using physics instead.
approach: The authors combined a standard image-dehazing technique (the dark channel prior) with atmospheric extinction theory, assuming a Marshall–Palmer raindrop size distribution. This yields equations linking image transmission, rainfall intensity and the distance to the background (scene depth), which can be inverted to estimate rainfall. They tested it with three low-cost interval cameras (one image per minute) on the banks of the Omu River in a mountainous watershed in Yamanashi, Japan, over 235 days from April to December 2021, against a 1-minute tipping-bucket gauge. Each image was split into 64 patches, and the scene depth of each patch was taken from a 5 m digital elevation model.
findings: As the theory predicts, image transmission dropped exponentially with both rainfall intensity and distance to the background.
For backgrounds farther than about 100 m, the derived extinction coefficients agreed with earlier studies; for closer backgrounds they were overestimated, with or without rain.

Rainfall errors depended strongly on the chosen background: restricting to patches beyond 100 m cut the median error to roughly 41–97% across the three cameras, whereas using all patches gave much larger errors.
The best-performing patches were vegetated slopes about 130–200 m away, and with them the method tracked short-term ups and downs in rainfall.

The method needs only a single daytime image plus scene depth and runs in under a minute per image, but it cannot yet separate fog from rain, does not work at night, and is sensitive to dew or raindrops on the lens.
relevance: Flash floods in small mountain and urban catchments often happen where there is no rain gauge close enough to warn people in time. Cities, roads and rivers in Korea are already covered by CCTV, so a physics-based method that reads rainfall from existing cameras could add thousands of 'free' rain sensors during monsoon and typhoon storms. The study is also an honest reminder that camera rainfall is still rough: choosing the right background matters a lot, and fog and night-time remain open problems that students can work on.

title: The ability of LSTM to model snowmelt versus rainfall generated floods
authors: Bakke, S. J., Barna, D. M., Engeland, K., Kolberg, S. A., Nordeide, S.

figure.caption: How often the simulated flood peak lands on the right day for snowmelt, mixed and rainfall floods, for the LSTM (a) and the operational HBV model (b). Green is the correct day; grey shades are peaks that come too early, purple shades too late.
figure.credit: Figure 5 from Bakke et al. (2026), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: A single LSTM trained on 200 Norwegian catchments simulated flood peaks better than the operational HBV model, but snowmelt floods remain much harder to time than rainfall floods for both models.
background: Flood models are usually scored on all floods lumped together, yet in cold regions a spring snowmelt flood and an autumn rainstorm flood are driven by very different processes and weather histories. A model can look good overall while doing poorly on one flood type. Few deep learning studies have checked LSTM skill separately for each flood-generating process, which matters for national forecasting services that face both.
approach: The Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE) trained one LSTM (NeuralHydrology, 270-day input sequences) on 200 near-natural catchments using daily precipitation and temperature from the 1 km SeNorge grid plus 21 static catchment attributes. Both the LSTM and the operational semi-distributed HBV model were trained or calibrated on 2009–2024 and evaluated on the unseen 1994–2009 period in 103 catchments. Floods were picked as independent peaks above the 98th percentile and labelled snowmelt, rainfall or mixed depending on whether more than two-thirds of the input water came from melt or rain. Peak timing, peak magnitude error, false alarm rate and probability of detection were compared for each flood type.
findings: Overall the LSTM reached an average NSE of 0.84 (HBV 0.76) and had a higher NSE in 99 of 103 catchments.

The LSTM put the peak on the correct day for 77% of rainfall floods, 67% of mixed floods and only 50% of snowmelt floods; HBV was 14–16 percentage points lower for every type, mostly because its peaks came too early.
Peak-magnitude skill was similar across flood types: close to half of LSTM peaks were within ±20%, versus about 36–38% for HBV, and both models tended to underestimate peaks.
Per catchment, the LSTM beat HBV on timing in 84% (snowmelt) and 78% (rainfall) of catchments, with the largest gains where HBV performed worst.
A remaining weakness is that the LSTM underestimates flow variability in most catchments (82%).
relevance: Deep learning models are moving from research papers into national flood warning services, and this study shows how to test them honestly: separately for each kind of flood rather than with one average score. The finding that snowmelt peaks are hard to time even for a strong LSTM is a useful reminder that a good overall score can hide weak spots. In Korea most floods come from monsoon rain and typhoons rather than snowmelt, but the same idea applies: models should be checked separately on convective downpours, typhoon rain and long rainy-season events before they are trusted for warnings, especially in small basins.

title: Observed Increase in the Spatial Extent of Extreme Precipitation Events Attributed to Anthropogenic Climate Change
authors: Zhang, Y., Liang, K., Liu, C.

figure.caption: Global land trends in the size of large extreme-rain events from 1982 to 2019 in three precipitation datasets: yearly anomalies of accumulated area (a) and projected area (b), and the trends broken down by continent (c, e) and by country (d, f), where blue marks growing and red marks shrinking footprints.
figure.credit: Figure 2 from Zhang et al. (2026), Water Resources Research, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Large extreme-rain events over the world's land have been covering more ground since the early 1980s, and climate model experiments point to greenhouse-gas warming as the main reason.
background: Most studies of extreme precipitation ask whether storms are getting more intense or more frequent, but how much area a single event covers also decides how bad the damage is: a widespread storm can flood several river basins at once and overwhelm emergency response. Earlier work on event size was mostly regional and gave conflicting answers, partly because each study used different data and definitions. A consistent global picture, and an explanation of what drives any change, was missing.
approach: The authors used three daily gridded precipitation datasets at 0.5° (CPC_Global, GPCC and the GSWP3-W5E5 reanalysis) for global land from 1982 to 2019. A grid-day counts as extreme when rain exceeds that cell's 95th percentile of wet days, and extreme cells that touch in space or on neighbouring days are linked into one event using a 3D (longitude–latitude–time) 26-connectivity method, similar to labelling connected objects in an image. They kept only large events (at least 100,000 km² of accumulated area and at least 2 days) and measured each event's 'accumulated area' (area counted once for every extreme day) and 'projected area' (its footprint on the map). Trends were estimated with Theil–Sen slopes and Mann–Kendall tests, and 11 CMIP6 models run with all forcings, natural forcing only, greenhouse gases only and aerosols only were compared to attribute the change.
findings: Roughly 1,000 large events per year were found (about 34,000–39,000 in total per dataset), and their average size grew in all three datasets: accumulated area by about 1,033–1,542 km² per year (0.32–0.43% per year) and projected area by about 840–1,237 km² per year (0.33–0.43% per year), all significant at p < 0.01.

Growth was consistent across datasets in South America, Oceania, Europe and Asia, with the strongest national increases in Brazil, China, Russia, Ukraine and Venezuela; only a few countries, such as Canada, Germany and Tanzania, showed shrinking events.

All 11 climate models reproduced an upward trend under historical forcing, while runs with only natural forcing (sun and volcanoes) showed almost no change, so the increase is attributed to human influence.
Greenhouse gases alone enlarged events (about 883 km² per year in accumulated area), while aerosols pushed the other way (about −167 km² per year), so the warming effect clearly dominates.

Accumulated area grew faster than projected area, suggesting events are becoming both wider and longer-lasting; the result held when thresholds were changed (90th percentile, ≥3 days, ≥50,000 km²) and when the period was cut to 1982–2014.
relevance: Flood design and warnings often treat heavy rain as a local, one-catchment problem, but this study shows that the footprint of extreme rain is itself growing, which raises the chance of several rivers flooding at the same time and stretching emergency services, insurance and reservoir operations across a whole region. Asia is one of the continents with the clearest increases (China among the strongest national trends), and Korea's monsoon fronts and typhoons are exactly the kind of large systems that can soak many basins at once. For students and engineers, the 3D connected-event idea is a simple, reusable way to look at storms as objects in space and time rather than as point rainfall totals.

title: Snow or rain? hybrid AI deciphers surface precipitation phase from satellite observations
authors: Yang, C., Li, H., Zhu, R., Wang, Y., Zhang, F., Gu, M., Jiang, G. M., Zhang, R., Tang, X.

figure.caption: How RePPIC-Net works: atmospheric profiles from the FuXi AI weather model feed a wet-bulb temperature step that decides rain or snow, while geostationary satellite images (observed, or extrapolated by the DaYu-FY model for nowcasting) feed a deep network that estimates intensity; the two are merged into a 0.05°, 15-minute rain/snow map.
figure.credit: Figure 7 from Yang et al. (2026), Nature Communications, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: By pairing a fast AI weather model with geostationary satellite images, RePPIC-Net maps whether it is raining or snowing, and how hard, within about two minutes instead of the roughly four-hour wait of current satellite products.
background: Whether precipitation reaches the ground as rain or snow decides whether a storm brings floods, blizzards, icy roads or avalanche danger, and the switch between the two can happen within hours. Ground gauges are sparse exactly where this matters most, in mountains and cold high-latitude regions, and they undercatch snow in wind. Satellite products such as GPM IMERG do separate rain from snow, but they arrive at least about four hours late and at coarser resolution, which is too slow for warnings.
approach: The authors built a hybrid system with two branches. For phase, 12-hour forecasts of temperature and humidity profiles from the AI weather model FuXi are interpolated to the terrain height and turned into wet-bulb temperature, which gives a probability of liquid precipitation using the same formula as IMERG. For intensity, a UNet first detects where it is precipitating and a ResUNet then estimates the rate from 15-minute infrared images of China's Fengyun-4B satellite, cloud-cluster features and FuXi fields, trained against GPM spaceborne radar from June 2022 to September 2023. Feeding in satellite images extrapolated by a transformer model (DaYu-FY) turns the system into a 1–3 hour nowcast. It was tested over two winters (October–March 2023–24 and 2024–25) against more than 2,000 weather stations in China and compared with GPM IMERG-Late and the official Fengyun-4B product.
findings: For light-to-moderate precipitation (0.1–5 mm/h), the combined detection-and-phase score (CSI-PD) for snowfall was 0.1574 versus 0.1001 for IMERG-Late, about 57% better; for rainfall it was 0.3147 versus 0.3064.

Over all precipitation, rain identification was similar to IMERG (CSI 0.85 vs. 0.83), while snow identification was slightly lower (0.69 vs. 0.71) because of false alarms at some stations; both products struggled with snow in southern China and during October and March transition months.
In a November 2023 cold-wave blizzard over northeast China, RePPIC-Net had the lowest intensity error (RMSE 1.65 mm/h) and a snowfall CSI-PD of 0.64 against 0.39 for IMERG.
With forecast satellite images as input, skill dropped only slightly over 1–3 hours (rain CSI-PD 0.29 to 0.27; snow 0.15 to 0.14), and the whole chain runs in about two minutes on one GPU.
Across the satellite's full disk, it reduced snowfall RMSE by 58% relative to the official Fengyun-4B product (0.19 vs. 0.46), though it still has regional biases near Antarctica and over oceans.
relevance: Korea's winters bring sudden heavy snow on the east coast and in mountain areas, and a storm that falls as rain in one valley can be snow a few hundred metres higher, which matters for road safety, roof collapse, avalanches and how quickly water runs off into rivers. This study shows that combining geostationary satellite images (like those from Korea's GK-2A) with fast AI weather models can give phase-aware precipitation maps in near real time, even where ground stations are scarce. It is also an honest reminder that snow in complex terrain and during season transitions remains hard, so such products should complement, not replace, ground observations and forecaster judgement.

title: Improving flood detection with large-scale dashboard camera data
authors: Franchi, M., Garg, N., Ju, W., Pierson, E.

figure.caption: The BayFlood pipeline as stacked map layers: raw dashcam images across New York City are labelled flooded or not flooded by a vision-language model, checked against external flood data (sensors, 311 reports, stormwater maps), and combined into a flood estimate for every Census tract.
figure.credit: Figure 1 from Franchi et al. (2026), Nature Communications, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Ordinary dashboard-camera photos, read by an off-the-shelf vision-language model and combined with a spatial Bayesian model, can map street flooding across a whole city and reveal flooded neighbourhoods that sensors and resident reports miss.
background: Cities usually learn where streets flood from three sources: fixed flood sensors, resident complaints (such as New York's 311 line) and physics-based stormwater maps. Sensors are too few to cover every street, complaints depend on who chooses to report, and stormwater maps assume rainfall that does not match any real storm. Dashcams on commercial and ride-share cars photograph streets continuously, but training a flood detector normally needs a large labelled dataset, which is hard to build because flooded images are rare.
approach: The authors used about 1.44 million dashcam images supplied by the company Nexar, mainly 926,212 daytime images from New York City during the 29 September 2023 storm, plus three other storm days in New York and the San Francisco Bay Area. Each image was classified without any task-specific training by the open-source vision-language model Cambrian-1-13B, which was asked whether the street showed more than a foot of standing water. One thousand of the classified images were checked by hand, and a spatial Bayesian model then combined the model labels, these human checks and nearby-tract information to estimate the fraction of flooded images in each Census tract. The resulting map was compared with 311 reports, FloodNet sensor locations, stormwater accumulation zones, catch basins and elevation.
findings: Only 0.2% of the New York images were classified as flooded; 65.8% of those were truly flooded, while just 0.6% of images classified as dry actually showed flooding, so a 'flooded' label made flooding about 110 times more likely.
The zero-shot model beat other open-source vision-language models, a fine-tuned ResNet and GPT-4o-mini, and kept strong signal on the other storm days and in San Francisco.

Tracts the method flagged as high risk were 1.9 times likelier to have a FloodNet sensor and 1.3 times likelier to have a 311 flood report, and their minimum elevation was 2.0 times lower, even though the model was not given these data.
About 1.05 million New Yorkers (12% of the city) live in high-risk tracts; 100,150 of them live where none of the existing methods (sensors, 311 or stormwater maps) indicated flood risk.

After accounting for estimated flooding, wealthier tracts and those with more White residents and fewer Hispanic residents were more likely to file 311 reports, and the authors used the maps to suggest 25 new sensor sites to the FloodNet team.
relevance: Urban flash floods, like those in Seoul's low-lying districts during intense monsoon downpours, often hit streets long before any gauge or official report notices them. This study shows that cameras already moving through the city, such as dashcams, CCTV or delivery vehicles, can act as a dense flood-monitoring network without costly labelling, and it reminds us that complaint-based data can under-represent vulnerable neighbourhoods. For students and engineers it is a practical template for combining AI image classification with simple statistics and a small amount of human checking; for city managers it points to fairer ways to choose where sensors and drainage upgrades go.

title: Short-term drought forecasting in Iran using multi-source machine learning: an assessment of autoregressive, teleconnection-driven, and hybrid paradigms
authors: Jian, J., Mahmoudi, P., Jafari, P., Ghaemi, A., Yang, J., Firoozi, F.
journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences

figure.caption: Workflow of the study: monthly rainfall is turned into the SPI drought index, combined with climate-index inputs under three scenarios, and fed to nine machine- and deep-learning models whose 1–3-month forecasts are scored with R², MSE and MAE.
figure.credit: Figure 3 from Jian et al. (2026), Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: For month-ahead drought forecasts in Iran, there is no single best recipe: mixing a station's own drought history with global climate indices works best in dry inland areas, while either source alone wins in certain coastal or local climates.
background: Drought forecasters usually pick one of two kinds of inputs: the recent history of the drought index itself (its 'memory'), or large-scale climate signals such as ENSO or the NAO that steer rainfall from far away. Each approach has worked in local case studies, but nobody had compared them, and their combination, side by side across a large and climatically diverse country. Iran, which ranges from hyper-arid deserts to very wet Caspian coasts, is a natural test bed for that question.
approach: The authors used 30 years (1993–2022) of quality-checked monthly rainfall from 96 synoptic stations and computed the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI). They built three input scenarios: S1 used 19 global teleconnection indices lagged 1–3 months; S2 used past SPI values with memory lengths of 3, 6, 9 or 12 months; S3 combined the climate indices with 3 or 6 months of SPI history. Nine algorithms, from linear regression and KNN to Random Forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, Bayesian ridge regression and LSTM, forecast SPI 1, 2 and 3 months ahead and were scored with R², MSE and MAE. They also repeated runs 20 times at two contrasting stations to check how stable each model was.
findings: With climate indices alone (S1), Random Forest was the most reliable model, and in the northwest, Caspian coast and western Zagros it explained up to about half of the SPI variance one month ahead (R² of 0.57 at Anzali), but skill dropped sharply at 2–3 months.
With drought history alone (S2), longer memory helped: feeding 12 months of past SPI gave the best results, and LSTM was the top model in this setting.
The hybrid setting (S3) won across much of the arid and semi-arid central plateau; at Isfahan it reached R² = 0.65 with MSE = 0.36, beating both single-source options.

Some places preferred a single source: climate indices worked best at Chabahar (R² = 0.49) and Anzali, while drought history alone was best at Ahvaz (R² = 0.55), and each station's winning setup rarely changed at longer lead times.
Across 20 repeated runs, Random Forest gave the most consistent scores, while LSTM and the polynomial SVM varied more from run to run.
relevance: Drought early warning is only useful if forecasts are trustworthy where people actually live and farm, and this study shows that the best forecasting setup can change from one region to the next. Korea faces a similar mix of influences, with monsoon rainfall, typhoons and dry springs shaped by both local persistence and large-scale signals like ENSO, so a 'one model for the whole country' approach may leave some basins poorly served. A practical lesson for students and water managers is to test several input designs and keep a simple, stable model such as Random Forest as a strong baseline before turning to more complex deep learning.

title: How well do hydrological models simulate streamflow extremes and drought-to-flood transitions?
authors: Muñoz-Castro, E., Anderson, B. J., Astagneau, P. C., Swain, D. L., Mendoza, P. A., Brunner, M. I.

figure.caption: Detected droughts (red shading), floods (blue) and the time between them: a rapid drought-to-flood transition in the Biobío River, Chile (a), and a seasonal one in the Dischma River, Switzerland (b).
figure.credit: Figure 3 from Muñoz-Castro et al. (2026), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: A model with a high KGE can still miss floods and drought-to-flood switches — extremes need to be checked on their own.
background: A drought that suddenly flips into a flood can do more damage than either extreme alone: dry soils, low reservoirs and drought-mode operations leave little room to respond. Hydrological models are the main tool for studying such transitions, but they are usually calibrated and judged with aggregate scores such as the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE), which say little about how well individual extreme events are reproduced.
approach: The authors calibrated four conceptual rainfall–runoff models (GR4J, GR5J, GR6J and TUW) in 63 catchments in Chile and Switzerland, trying several calibration set-ups: KGE variants, streamflow transformations and component weights. Droughts and floods were picked out with thresholds, a transition was defined as a drought followed by a flood within a set window (rapid: under 14 days; seasonal: under 90 days), and detection skill was scored with the Critical Success Index (CSI). ANOVA and correlation analysis then separated the effects of model structure, calibration choices and catchment attributes.
findings: A high KGE does not guarantee good event detection: median CSI was around 0.5 for droughts but only about 0.2–0.3 for floods and for transitions.
Droughts are captured better than floods, rapid (under 14-day) transitions are the hardest, and skill depends mainly on getting the timing right.
Model structure matters most, followed by the streamflow transformation used in calibration; the KGE formulation and weights matter less.
Skill is lowest in semi-arid, high-mountain and flashy catchments, pointing to weak representation of soil-moisture and near-surface processes.
relevance: Flood warnings, drought plans and climate-impact studies all lean on hydrological models, so a model that looks good on average but misses the extremes can give false confidence exactly when it matters. In Korea, dry springs that switch into heavy monsoon floods are a familiar pattern, and this kind of transition is where the paper finds models weakest. For anyone building or using such models — students, researchers or water managers — the lesson is simple: check the extremes and the switches between them directly, not just the overall score.
